blk_part_01_what_a_quantum_computer_is.text: A quantum computer uses qubits, short for quantum bits. A qubit is a tiny physical thing, such as a very small electric part or a single atom. A qubit can be in superposition: a mix of 0 and 1 at the same time, until we measure it. Picture a coin spinning on a table. While it spins, it is not heads or tails. When it stops, it becomes one of them. Measuring a qubit is like stopping the coin: the superposition ends, and you get a normal 0 or 1.

Now picture two linked coins. Nobody knows how they will land. In one simple case, every time one lands on heads, the other lands on heads too. Other links are possible, for example one heads and the other tails. Entanglement lets many qubits work as one big system instead of many separate parts.

blk_part_02_why_it_is_so_hard_to_build.text: The solution is error correction: the information of one reliable qubit is spread across many physical qubits. The physical qubits are the real, noisy ones in the machine. Together they make one logical qubit, the reliable one that the program uses. Some extra qubits keep checking whether their neighbors still agree, without reading the information itself. When a check shows a problem, a normal computer works out which qubit went wrong and corrects it. This way, the logical qubit can keep its information longer than any one of its physical qubits.

blk_part_05_how_ai_really_helps.text: The second job is tuning. A quantum computer has many control settings, like the knobs on an old radio. These settings slowly move away from their best values. Today, automatic programs and experts set them. To fix the slow change, the error checks must stop for a new setup. Google researchers built an AI agent that uses reinforcement learning. This means it gets better by trying things and getting a reward. It keeps changing more than a thousand settings while the machine keeps working. So the error checks do not need to stop. It uses the error checks as its score. In their tests, it reduced the logical error rate by about 20 percent more. This was on a machine already set by programs and experts.

In an error-corrected machine, one kind of step, the T gate, costs much more than the others. The machine cannot do this step reliably in the normal way. So each T gate needs many extra qubits and extra steps. Google DeepMind and Quantinuum presented AlphaTensor-Quantum. This AI rewrites the circuits so that they need fewer T gates. On some tests, it cut their number by half or more. Fewer expensive steps mean that a machine can do useful work sooner.

blk_part_05_how_ai_really_helps.text: Will quantum computers make AI better? The answer today is: mostly unknown. In 2025, the bank HSBC and IBM reported better test scores for a machine-learning model. The model learned from trading data that was changed on a real IBM quantum computer. It was one small study, not proof that quantum computers make AI better in general. One big problem is data. AI learns from huge amounts of data, and putting that data into qubits is slow. This can use up the time that a quantum computer saves.
